solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Voice of inferior quality? Sounds like it

indicators.note: 'Sounds like it' says the answer is said the same as the phrase before it

blocks.note: base means low-grade or inferior; the spelling changes to the singing voice while the sound stays

explanation.surface: A critic sneering at a poor singer: that voice was second-rate, and you could hear it.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the whole first half as a single definition-and-pun: BASS is a voice, and it is pronounced exactly like BASE.
explanation.definitionFit: A bass is the lowest male singing voice.

clue.text: In the morning I depart leaving friend

blocks.note: AM, ante meridiem, is the morning
taken as printed
to depart is to go

explanation.surface: Someone slipping away early in the morning, leaving a friend behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaving' looks like an instruction to drop letters, but here it only joins: the wordplay leaves, or yields, the friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for friend, and common in English as a casual word for a pal.

clue.text: Modern gallery in the quiet centre

blocks.note: the Tate is the London art gallery
quiet in the sense of soft, not loud
the heart of something is its centre

explanation.surface: A calm, modern gallery tucked in the middle of a quiet town.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is London's national art gallery (Tate Modern holds its modern collection). The word breaks in the wordplay fall nowhere near the answer's own word breaks, which hides the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: State of the art means the most modern and up to date.

clue.text: Perfect print to order

blocks.note: a print is a copy
to order a table or tickets is to book them

explanation.surface: A printer turning out flawless copies made to order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect' is an adjective here, so the answer is COPYBOOK used as an adjective, as in 'a copybook landing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Copybook as an adjective means exactly correct, like the model handwriting in an old copybook.

clue.text: Top title

blocks.note: the highest part of the head, or of a hill or a hat
a championship title, as won by a boxing champion

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it looks like 'best title'; split it, and each word is its own meaning of CROWN.
explanation.definitionFit: The crown is the top of the head or a hill, and a crown is a championship title, as in the world crown.

clue.text: I make mistake filling cup for clown

blocks.note: a pot is a cup, as in a sporting trophy
I plus ERR, to make a mistake

explanation.surface: A clumsy clown spilling into the cup and owning up to it.
explanation.walkthrough: P(I ERR)OT: 'I make mistake' reads as I ERR, and that fills the POT.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierrot is the sad white-faced clown of French pantomime.

clue.text: A bit hasty, mate shot nevertheless

indicators.note: shot means ruined or wrecked, so the letters are broken up

blocks.note: all thirteen letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A friend who fired a bit too quickly, but it was still a decent shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like the noun ending the surface story, but it is the signal that the preceding letters are scrambled.
explanation.definitionFit: Be that as it may is a phrase meaning nevertheless or even so.

clue.text: Work at home on island, on view

blocks.note: OP is short for opus, a work
someone at home is in
I is the abbreviation for island
the second 'on', taken as printed

explanation.surface: Someone working from home on an island with a fine view.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue has two 'on's doing different jobs: the first only joins the pieces, the second is kept as printed, so the definition is the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what you think of something is your view of it, as in 'in my view'.

clue.text: Protective garment needed by chap in a forest

indicators.note: the answer sits in the run of letters that follows

blocks.note: chaP IN A FOREst

explanation.surface: A man in the woods who needs something to protect his clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'in' of the surface does double duty: it signals the hiding and is also part of the hidden letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinafore is an apron-like garment worn to keep clothes clean.

clue.text: Helpful hint about river excursion

blocks.note: a tip is a helpful hint
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Useful advice for a day out on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' sits between the hint and the river, so it reads as 'concerning'; it actually wraps the hint around R.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a short journey out and back for pleasure.

clue.text: Travel with the French writer almost direct

blocks.note: to travel is to go
Jules VERNE, the French novelist, without his final E

explanation.surface: Heading off on a journey with Jules Verne, nearly in charge of the route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French' looks like a request for LE or LA; here it simply describes the writer, Jules Verne, author of Around the World in Eighty Days.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to rule or steer the course of a country or organisation.

clue.text: Mostly wise over fossil fuel

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means turned upside down

blocks.note: SAGE, wise, less its last letter

explanation.surface: A sensible reflection on the fuel debate, mostly.
explanation.walkthrough: SAGE loses its E to become SAG, and that reads upwards as GAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: natural gas, like coal and oil, formed from ancient buried organisms.

clue.text: Radio broadcast my English band crewmember

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are strewn about

blocks.note: taken as printed
surface padding: an exclamation of surprise that adds no letters
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A radio show about someone who works behind the scenes for an English band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Radio broadcast' reads as one natural phrase, which hides that 'broadcast' is working on RADIO plus E.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadie is a member of the crew that tours with a band, setting up its equipment.

clue.text: Free snifters later – willpower’s required!

indicators.note: the letters are set free from their order

blocks.note: all thirteen letters are rearranged
surface padding after the definition, completing the exclamation

explanation.surface: Free drinks on offer later, so someone will need to hold back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free' looks like it describes the drinks, but it is the signal to rearrange them; a snifter is a small drink of spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-restraint is willpower, the ability to hold back.

clue.text: Causing strong feelings in European grounds

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
grounds for doing something are a motive

explanation.surface: Stirring emotions at a European football ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grounds' suggests stadiums, but it means reasons, as in grounds for divorce.
explanation.definitionFit: Emotive means arousing strong feeling.

clue.text: Unreliable boy holding sailor up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a boy's name
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A flaky lad propping up a sailor, perhaps after a night out.
explanation.walkthrough: TAR goes up to RAT, and ERIC holds it: ER(RAT)IC.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something that behaves irregularly cannot be depended on.

clue.text: Be all square in match

blocks.note: a verb: to finish level on points
a noun: a game in a knockout competition, as in the FA Cup

explanation.walkthrough: 'In match' looks like part of one sporting phrase, but 'match' is a second definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: To tie is to finish level, all square; a tie is also a match in a knockout competition, as in a cup tie.

clue.text: Test that woman, one who’s given birth

blocks.note: the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for cars in Britain
her refers to that woman

explanation.surface: A medical check for a woman who has just had a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: The MOT is the British yearly test that every older car must pass to stay on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the phrase describes the answer's defining trait rather than giving a synonym.

clue.text: A Royal son finally put in charge

blocks.note: a charge is a price
the last letter of son

explanation.surface: A royal son at last given responsibility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put in charge' reads as one idiom for being given authority; split it, and N is put in PRICE.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: 'A Royal' is a member of the royal family, usually a monarch's son here.

clue.text: Change pound before church

blocks.note: a pound is an enclosure for animals, a pen
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Converting pounds into coins for the church collection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' with 'Change' suggests money, but here it is an animal enclosure; the money is in the answer, pence being small British coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Change is small coins, and pence are British coins, a hundred to the pound.

clue.text: Member of the clergy caught on immediately

blocks.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
anon is an old word for at once, immediately

explanation.surface: A cleric who picked up on something straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' is part of the second fragment, not a link: 'anon' is an archaic word meaning straight away.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is one particular rank of cleric, one on the staff of a cathedral.

clue.text: Operatic star eager to return

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: avid means eager

explanation.surface: A famous soprano keen to make a comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: AVID read backwards is DIVA.
explanation.definitionFit: A diva is a celebrated female opera singer.

clue.text: Principle involving guys in the flat

blocks.note: a tenet is a principle
guys are men

explanation.surface: House rules for the blokes sharing a flat.
explanation.walkthrough: TENE(MEN)T. In Scotland a tenement is a flat in a large shared building, which is what makes 'flat' fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenement is a flat or apartment, especially one in a large old block.

clue.text: A nettle blown about court arm

blocks.note: A NETTLE rearranged
the first letter of court, abbreviating it

explanation.surface: A nettle blowing around a tennis court and stinging someone's arm.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one letter of 'court' is used: its first, as in the abbreviation Ct. 'Arm' is a limb here, not a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A tentacle is the long flexible arm of an octopus or squid.

clue.text: Pull bovine animal across rear of barn

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: a yak is a long-haired ox
the last letter of barn

explanation.surface: Dragging an ox round the back of the barn.
explanation.walkthrough: YA(N)K: the yak stretches across the N.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb, with the added sense of a sudden hard tug.
